content: An initial review of the literature did not identify any studies or trials that directly compared the outcomes of different toxicity monitoring strategies for tenofovir and entecavir. The review instead focused on the long-term renal adverse effects associated with these drugs in both nucleoside-naïve and nucleoside-experienced patients. Eight studies involving adults treated with tenofovir were included, two of which involved patients co-infected with HBV and HIV. Four studies examined entecavir-treated patients. No studies were identified in children. The evidence quality was rated very low, as the data were derived from non-controlled observational studies. No studies have compared monitoring strategies for tenofovir, such as routine toxicity monitoring versus no monitoring or targeted monitoring based on clinical need. The DART clinical trial in HIV-infected adults compared laboratory and clinical monitoring and found that tenofovir use was associated with an increased risk of reduced eGFR but no increased risk of renal failure over a median follow-up of five years. This evidence was of low quality. Several prospective studies reported renal function outcomes after 2–5 years of tenofovir treatment. At five years, less than 1% of individuals had elevated serum creatinine levels or decreased CrCl or serum phosphate levels. Among patients with decompensated liver disease, 9% treated with tenofovir for 48 weeks experienced increased serum creatinine levels, but treatment discontinuation was rare. Long-term studies (3–5 years) on entecavir reported limited adverse outcomes. Six percent of patients on entecavir monotherapy showed increased serum creatinine levels over 96 weeks. In HBV/HIV co-infected individuals, the incidence of tenofovir-related kidney dysfunction was low in the short to medium term, despite a high prevalence of chronic kidney disease in this population. Independent risk factors for decreased GFR in HBV-monoinfected and HBV/HIV-co-infected patients included older age, non-African origin, lower baseline eGFR, longer tenofovir therapy duration, and HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/mL. In children and adolescents, tenofovir-related decreases in bone mineral density (BMD) have been observed, but the clinical significance of these changes, particularly with prolonged therapy, remains unclear. In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of adolescents aged 12–18 years, no patient met the safety endpoint of a 6% decrease in spine BMD at week 72. There is uncertainty about the best methods to measure and monitor tenofovir-related bone toxicity in children. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) testing is not widely available and does not detect osteomalacia. Careful growth monitoring is recommended for children on tenofovir therapy. The safety profile of entecavir in children was consistent with that in adults, with no renal adverse events reported over 48 weeks in an ongoing trial. There is limited data on optimal assays for monitoring tenofovir-related nephrotoxicity. Some individuals may have normal serum creatinine levels but impaired renal function, suggesting that reliance on absolute serum creatinine values may lead to tenofovir administration in patients with pre-existing kidney disease. Glycosuria has been observed in non-diabetic individuals with tenofovir nephrotoxicity, suggesting that urine dipstick testing for glycosuria may be a cost-effective screening tool for serious tenofovir-induced kidney injury. The Guidelines Development Group recommended baseline renal function assessment and risk categorization for renal dysfunction in HBV-monoinfected individuals, as well as annual renal function and growth monitoring in children. Monitoring renal function to detect changes in eGFR after initiating tenofovir therapy is important to prevent kidney disease progression, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) with limited access to dialysis. For low-risk individuals, periodic renal function monitoring every 12 months was recommended. For high-risk individuals (e.g., older age, underlying renal disease, diabetes, hypertension, or concomitant nephrotoxic drugs), more frequent monitoring was advised. Most cases of tubular dysfunction are reversible, and dose adjustments based on renal function monitoring can reduce the risk of renal impairment. The renal toxicity of tenofovir primarily affects the renal tubules, and glomerular function tests do not adequately measure tubular dysfunction. There are currently no simple tests to detect renal tubular toxicity. Monitoring may include serum creatinine, estimated GFR (eGFR) using the MDRD formula, serum phosphate, and urine dipstick tests for proteinuria and glycosuria. Growth monitoring is recommended for children and adolescents on tenofovir therapy. Resource considerations include the increased costs of long-term monitoring of serum creatinine, serum phosphate, and BMD scanning. Access to creatinine testing may be limited in some settings, and urine dipstick testing offers a simpler and cheaper alternative in LMICs. Challenges also exist in providing appropriate laboratory infrastructure and human resources for lifelong therapy and follow-up. Research gaps include evaluating the cost-effectiveness of routine laboratory screening for renal function in all individuals on long-term tenofovir and entecavir versus high-risk populations, developing simplified monitoring tools, and establishing the long-term safety and efficacy of tenofovir alafenamide versus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in HBV-monoinfected and HBV/HIV-co-infected populations. Chronic HBV infection increases the risk of death from liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with an estimated 650,000 annual deaths from HCC. In resource-limited settings, HBV is often diagnosed only when patients present with advanced HCC. Surveillance is required to detect HCC at an early stage (tumor size <3 cm) to improve treatment outcomes. Effective surveillance programs require access to treatments for small HCCs, such as alcohol injection or radiofrequency ablation, particularly in LMICs where liver transplantation or resection is limited. Current surveillance tools include ultrasound and/or alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) measurement, but there is no consensus on the best strategy or frequency for HCC monitoring in chronic HBV patients. Semi-annual surveillance has been shown to detect HCC at an earlier stage and improve survival. Risk factors for HCC include cirrhosis, HBeAg positivity, high HBV DNA levels, family history of HCC, age >40 years, elevated ALT levels, and HIV or HCV co-infection. Risk calculators have been developed to predict HCC risk based on factors such as age, sex, albumin, bilirubin, ALT, HBeAg status, HBV DNA levels, and cirrhosis. These models are largely derived from Asian patient cohorts.
